---
title: "Dynamic data: relationships through change"
toc: true
---

**Practical notebook.** Compute snapshot persistence for a changing point
cloud and inspect Betti summaries across time and scale. <a href="../../downloads/topic-06-participant.ipynb" download="topic-06-participant.ipynb">Download the notebook</a>.

Dynamic data add a second question to the persistent homology pipeline. We
must decide not only what structure to calculate within each observation, but
also what relationship, if any, connects observations through change.

A sequence of snapshot diagrams can show that topological summaries change.
It does not say that a point in $D_t$ and a nearby point in $D_{t+1}$ are the
same feature.

Going beyond snapshots requires additional structure. Different methods encode
different kinds of relationship:

| Scientific need | Mathematical route | Structure that must be justified |
|---|---|---|
| compare changing summaries | snapshot persistence | comparable frames or windows |
| follow known agents or cells | track observations first | reliable identities or correspondence |
| represent additions and removals | zigzag persistence | inclusions that can point forwards or backwards |
| retain two ordered construction choices | multiparameter persistence | compatible maps in both parameter directions |
| follow persistence pairings along controlled change | vineyard | a specified path of filtrations |

These methods are not ranked from basic to superior. Each makes a stronger
claim because it assumes a stronger relationship.

::: {.column-margin .study-note .insight}
**Identity needs evidence.** Timestamps order observations but do not create
feature identity. Any claim that a component, loop or cavity is the same one
later must come from tracking, inclusions or another stated correspondence.
:::

::: {.column-margin .study-note .qualification}
**Two axes are not enough.** A heat map over physical time and filtration
scale is a useful Betti surface. It becomes a two-parameter persistence module
only when both directions carry compatible maps.
:::

## Observation identity comes first when it is available

Tracked particles, cells or agents can support a changing graph or a fixed
ambient scaffold. Their labels do not automatically identify homology
classes, but they provide information absent from unlabelled snapshots.

When trajectories cross, observations enter or leave, or detections are
missing, nearest-neighbour matching can invent continuity. Any later claim
about a persistent topological feature is then conditional on that tracking
model.

## Zigzag persistence: allow structure to enter and leave

Ordinary persistence follows nested growth. A zigzag permits inclusions in
both displayed directions:

$$
K_0\longrightarrow K_1\longleftarrow K_2
\longrightarrow K_3\longleftarrow\cdots.
$$

This is useful when complexes gain and lose simplices but can still be related
through meaningful inclusions. Finite zigzag modules retain an interval
decomposition, so their lifetimes can still be represented by a barcode
[@carlsson2010zigzag].

For example, a path may gain one closing edge and later lose it. The loop
exists only in the middle complex. The arrows distinguish this connected
event from three unrelated Betti-number calculations.

## Multiparameter persistence: retain two ordered choices

Scale and density, distance and interaction order, or threshold and spatial
resolution may both define inclusions. A multiparameter module retains those
directions rather than imposing an artificial total ordering. General
multiparameter modules do not admit the complete interval-barcode
classification available in one parameter [@carlsson2009multidimensional].
Rank invariants, slices and dimension functions therefore summarise selected
aspects rather than completely classifying the object.

Independent time snapshots do not generally form this structure. Time can be
an ordered parameter when observations accumulate or another construction
supplies genuine inclusions.

## Vineyards: follow pairings along a path of filtrations

Suppose a fixed complex $K$ carries a filtration function $f_t$ that changes
with external time $t$. Each $f_t$ produces one persistence diagram. A
vineyard follows its persistence points along the specified path of
filtrations, producing curves called vines [@cohensteiner2006vineyards].

![Persistence points move through external time and trace vines.](../../assets/vineyard-animation.svg){fig-alt="A time cursor changes filtration values while two points move through a persistence diagram and trace two vines."}

External time selects the current filtration. Birth and death coordinates
remain values of the filtration parameter, not timestamps.

::: {.column-margin .study-note .insight}
**Why a vineyard is more than a stack.** The path of changing filtration
values determines a sequence of ordering events in the filtered complex. The
algorithm updates persistence pairings through those events rather than
joining whichever plotted points happen to be nearest.
:::

A fixed mesh carrying a changing field or a fixed interaction complex with
changing weights is a natural vineyard setting. A Rips complex of freely
moving points is more delicate because many distances and simplices can
exchange order.
